name: Abel Weir
description: Sergeant of the City Watch, forty-one, twenty-two years in blue-grey. Keeps the referral book at the Isle post -- four inches of complaints against the Baron's people that he has been ordered to record and not act on. He is very tired.
narrative:
Twenty-two years of drunks, cutpurses and canal-right disputes, and Abel Weir has
never once had to decide whether he was a coward. The standing order made that a
daily question and he has been answering it wrong since it came down, in writing,
in a neat hand, in a book.

He is not a hero and he will not draw on a Dragon Knight in the street. What he
will do is *keep the record* -- names, dates, witnesses, the barrow-man's broken
jaw, the two boatmen who did not come back -- and he has begun to understand that
the record is worth something to somebody with the standing to use it.

**Use him** as the party's lawful door. He cannot accuse a lord and he cannot lay a hand on a Knight -- a sergeant who tried would be ruined, and he knows the arithmetic exactly. He can produce
a written, dated, witnessed account of every offence committed in this city in the
last eight days, to the right person, and he badly wants to. He needs it to be
someone else's decision.

**He will recognise a professional.** Anyone who has held a warrant anywhere -- an
Order investigator, a watch captain out of Anminster, a Sword of the Lake -- gets
the book opened for them faster than any amount of Influence.

**What he is afraid of:** not the Knights. Being the sergeant whose name is on the
disobedience when it all goes wrong, with a wife and two daughters on Isle post
pay.

equipment.name: Watch baton
equipment.notes: Not a weapon of war and he knows it.

equipment.name: The referral book
equipment.notes: Four inches thick. Every complaint against the Baron's people since the column arrived: names, dates, witnesses, injuries. Recorded and referred, not acted upon. It is the single most useful object in the city for anyone trying to make the occupation a legal problem -- and he will not hand it over without being given a reason he can live with.

actor_notes:
Abel Weir
BODY: Forty-one, heavy, tired, blue-grey coat. A four-inch book under one arm that he does not put down, not to eat, not to drink. Stands at the edge of a street where he can see all of it.
BUSINESS: Writing. The book comes open, the pencil comes out, names and hours go down in a neat hand — and then the book closes and he walks away, and that is the worst thing in the scene.
LISTENS: Taking it down. He will ask you to repeat a name so he can spell it correctly, and the ordinariness of that is what breaks people.
WANTS: To put the book in front of somebody who can use it without being the man who disobeyed.
GUARDS: That he is ashamed. Hides it in procedure — the entry number, the date, the two witnesses.
BREAKS: He stops writing while you are still talking, and looks at you, and the pencil stays where it is.
KEY: "Thirty-one entries. I can tell you all of them from memory and not one of them has been answered."
